items.question: What kind of projects do you take on?
items.answer: Web apps, APIs and internal tools, from a first MVP to new features on a mature product. If it runs in a browser or behind one, I can probably help.

items.question: Why hire an independent engineer over an agency?
items.answer: You talk directly to the person writing the code. Decisions are faster, nothing gets lost in handoffs, and you pay for engineering rather than overhead.

items.question: Can you join an existing codebase?
items.answer: Yes. I start by reading the code, running it locally and shipping a small fix, so we both learn how the project works before taking on bigger pieces.

items.question: How long does a typical project take?
items.answer: Small features land within days. A first release of a new product usually takes four to eight weeks, with a timeline agreed before work starts.

items.question: Do you take on one-off projects?
items.answer: Yes. Fixed-scope projects get a clear price, a clear timeline and the same care as ongoing work.

posts.title: Designing APIs that last
posts.excerpt: Endpoints outlive the screens that first call them. Here is how I design APIs that are still pleasant to use years later.

sections.title: Start From the Client
paragraphs: Before writing a route, I write the code that will call it. If the request is awkward to build or the response needs three follow-up calls, the design is wrong, and it is far cheaper to find out now.
That habit keeps endpoints small and shaped around real tasks rather than database tables.

images.alt: Green and amber streaks of fast motion

sections.title: Name Things Once
paragraphs: Every concept gets one name across the database, the API and the interface. When a field is called status in one place and state in another, every new developer pays for it.
A short glossary in the repository settles arguments before they reach code review.

images.alt: A calm sea horizon at dusk

sections.title: Version by Addition
paragraphs: Most breaking changes can be avoided by adding instead of changing. New fields are optional, old fields stay until nothing reads them, and deprecations are announced with dates.

images.alt: Concrete blocks against a pale sky

sections.title: Test the Contract
paragraphs: Types catch typos, but contract tests catch broken promises. I keep a small suite that calls the API the way real clients do and fails loudly when a response changes shape.
Generated client types from the OpenAPI schema close the loop, so the frontend learns about a change at build time instead of in production.

posts.title: The case for less JavaScript
posts.excerpt: Every kilobyte has to be downloaded, parsed and run on someone’s phone. Shipping less is the fastest optimisation there is.

cover.alt: Concrete blocks against a pale sky

sections.title: Render on the Server
paragraphs: Most of a page never changes after it loads. Rendering that part on the server means visitors see content immediately and their phones never download the code that produced it.

images.alt: Monochrome light falling across a dark fold
A white fold on a pale grey ground

sections.title: Islands of Interaction
paragraphs: Interactivity goes where it is needed and nowhere else: a menu, a form, a carousel. Each island loads its own small bundle, and a slow widget never blocks the rest of the page.

images.alt: A cream fold catching warm light

sections.title: Measure on Real Phones
paragraphs: A fast laptop hides problems. I test on a mid-range phone over a throttled connection, because that is what many visitors actually use.
Core Web Vitals from real sessions are the scoreboard, not a lab score on a developer machine.

posts.title: Shipping on a small budget
posts.excerpt: You do not need a platform team to deploy safely. A few boring choices go a long way when every hour and every dollar counts.

cover.alt: A cream fold catching warm light

sections.title: Pick Managed Services
paragraphs: A managed database and a managed host cost a little more per month and save days every quarter. Patching servers is rarely the best use of a small team.

images.alt: Light beams converging in the dark
A dark vase on a wooden bench

sections.title: Automate the Path to Production
paragraphs: Every push runs lint, type checks, tests and a build. When all four pass, the same pipeline deploys. Releases become routine instead of events.

images.alt: Dusk light over a pool and dark walls

sections.title: Watch What Matters
paragraphs: Three alerts cover most problems: errors are up, the site is slow, or a background job stopped. Anything noisier gets ignored, so I keep the list short.

posts.title: Choosing a stack that lasts
posts.excerpt: The best stack is the one your team can still hire for, debug and upgrade in three years. Fashion is a poor guide.

cover.alt: Red light blurred across a pale ground

sections.title: Boring Is a Feature
paragraphs: Mature tools have answers for problems you have not met yet. I reach for proven foundations and save experiments for places where they can fail safely.

images.alt: Two dark forms in deep red light
Red light blurred across a pale ground

sections.title: Fewer Moving Parts
paragraphs: Each new service, queue or language is something to deploy, monitor and learn. A single well-structured app often beats a constellation of tiny ones for a small team.

sections.title: Plan the Upgrade
paragraphs: Frameworks change every year. Pinning versions, reading release notes and upgrading in small steps keeps a codebase current without heroic rewrites.
